42880961.text: Prior oncologic PET/MRI repeatability studies have been limited by single-center designs, small cohorts, or select patient populations. Our primary aim was to estimate the test-retest repeatability of uptake metrics on [18F]FDG PET/MRI studies across a variety of cancer types. A secondary aim was to assess the impact of intersession μ-map variability on repeatability. Methods: In this prospective study involving 2 institutions with different PET/MRI scanners, subjects completing standard-of-care [18F]FDG PET/CT or MRI examinations were recruited to undergo 2 research [18F]FDG PET/MRIs (i.e., test and retest) within a 1-9 d period per Quantitative Imaging Biomarker Alliance specifications. Enrollment required at least 1 measurable lesion (long axis ≥ 2 cm, known or expected SUVmax ≥ 4.0) and no active oncologic therapy. SUVmax and SUVpeak were extracted from measurable lesions (1-5 per subject). At site 1, attenuation-coefficient maps (i.e., μ-maps) were inspected for substantial differences across sessions. Additionally, at site 1, the retest μ-map was coregistered to the test μ-map, and the PET attenuation-correction process was repeated for the test session based on the retest μ-map. Intersession repeatability was assessed via Bland-Altman plots, and within-subject coefficients of variation (wCVs) were calculated. Results: At site 1, 10 subjects with 11 measurable lesions were analyzed, and the wCVs for SUVmax and SUVpeak were 12.3% and 9.6%, respectively. At site 2, 11 subjects with 30 measurable lesions were analyzed, and the wCVs for SUVmax and SUVpeak were 9.5% and 8.8%, respectively. At site 1, repeating attenuation correction of the test PET data with the retest μ-map slightly improved repeatability, reducing the wCV to 10.1% for SUVmax and to 9.1% for SUVpeak For 8 of 11 lesions at site 1, the μ-map substitution altered the test-retest change by less than 5%, with no appreciable intersession μ-map differences or artifacts. Conclusion: The test-retest repeatability of SUVmax among hypermetabolic lesions on [18F]FDG PET/MRI, using data from 2 scanner models, was similar to the Quantitative Imaging Biomarker Alliance's wCV benchmark of 10%-12% for [18F]FDG PET/CT. Intersession μ-map variations had minimal negative impact on repeatability.

42912561.text: 68 Ga-PSMA-11-PET/CT is widely used for staging prostate cancer but may also detect nonprostatic malignancies owing to prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) expression in tumor neovasculature. Here, we report a case of a newly diagnosed high-risk prostate adenocarcinoma that underwent staging 68 Ga-PSMA-11-PET/CT. In addition to the primary prostatic lesion, PSMA-expressing lesions were identified in the sternum and right thyroid lobe. While skeletal involvement was initially presumed metastatic prostate cancer, further evaluation revealed follicular variant papillary thyroid carcinoma. This case highlights an important diagnostic pitfall and demonstrates the value of PSMA-PET/CT in uncovering clinically occult synchronous malignancies.

42944911.text: Pancreatic cystic lesions (PCLs) are increasingly encountered in clinical practice owing to the widespread use of high-resolution cross-sectional imaging. These lesions comprise a heterogeneous group of entities ranging from benign cysts to pre-malignant neoplasms and invasive cancers, making accurate characterization essential for appropriate patient surveillance and therapeutic management. Imaging plays a pivotal role in lesion detection, differential diagnosis, and assessment of malignant potential. This review presents a practical imaging-based classification of PCLs founded on lesion morphology, relationship to the pancreatic ductal system, enhancement patterns, and associated imaging features. Using a stepwise diagnostic approach, pancreatic cystic lesions are categorized according to their increasing risk of malignancy into non-neoplastic cysts, serous cystic neoplasms, mucinous cystic lesions, and cystic degeneration of solid pancreatic tumors. Characteristic imaging findings, relevant differential diagnostic considerations, and imaging features associated with increased malignant potential are comprehensively reviewed, with particular emphasis on the role of MRI and MR cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) in lesion characterization. A structured pattern-recognition flowchart is proposed to facilitate routine image interpretation and enhance diagnostic confidence. In addition, a practical reporting template is presented to promote standardized assessment and effective communication within multidisciplinary teams. Emerging techniques, including diffusion-weighted imaging, quantitative MRI biomarkers, radiomics, artificial intelligence, and molecular analysis of cyst fluid, are discussed as promising tools for improving diagnostic accuracy and refining risk stratification. By emphasizing readily recognizable imaging features and a systematic diagnostic workflow, this review provides radiologists with a practical and clinically applicable framework for the evaluation, diagnosis, risk assessment, and multidisciplinary management of pancreatic cystic lesions.

42957211.text: We characterized patterns of treatment response and progression during [177Lu]Lu-PSMA radiopharmaceutical therapy (RPT) using serial posttreatment SPECT/CT and prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) PET imaging and evaluated cycle-by-cycle prostate-specific antigen (PSA)-imaging concordance. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 361 patients from 2 academic centers who received at least 2 cycles of [177Lu]Lu-PSMA RPT between May 2017 and March 2025. Posttreatment SPECT/CT scans were qualitatively evaluated to determine the site and pattern of response and progression, including PSMA low-avidity and PSMA-negative disease. Progression was defined by the appearance of new lesions or at least a 2-fold growth in preexisting lesions on SPECT/CT. PSA response was defined per Prostate Cancer Clinical Trials Working Group 3 criteria as at least a 50% decline from baseline. For cycle-by-cycle concordance analysis, PSA change was classified directionally as rising or falling relative to the prior cycle. In patients who paused or completed RPT after response, progression imaging was compared with the final on-treatment SPECT/CT scan. Results: Overall, 290 of 361 (80%) patients demonstrated a decrease in lesion size or number on posttreatment imaging. Of 312 patients with baseline bone disease, 81% demonstrated a response on posttreatment imaging. In total, 156 of 361 patients (43%) demonstrated progression during treatment. New osseous lesions developed in 132 patients, of whom 89 (67%) had PSMA low-avidity disease. At cycle 2, 64% of new lesions were osseous, increasing to at least 90% by cycles 4-6. PSMA-negative progression occurred in 22 patients (6%), predominantly in the liver (n = 11) and lymph nodes (n = 8), with 59% detected at cycle 2. Among 81 patients with imaging available at PSA progression after treatment completion or pause, 74 (91%) had imaging progression; of these, 69 (93%) demonstrated osseous and 13 (18%) nodal progression. PSA and imaging were discordant in 25%-43% of patients across cycles, with discordance increasing from cycle 2 to cycle 6. Conclusion: Progression during [177Lu]Lu-PSMA RPT occurs most frequently in bone, with 67% of patients with new osseous lesions demonstrating a PSMA low-avidity disease component. PSMA-negative progression is uncommon and tends to emerge early. PSA-imaging discordance is frequent, underscoring the need for integrated imaging assessment throughout treatment.

42970161.label: Objective
42970161.text: This study aimed to assess the effectiveness of the Node Reporting and Data System version 1.0 (Node-RADS 1.0) for preoperative evaluation of lymph node metastasis (LNM) in colon cancer and to benchmark its diagnostic performance against conventional CT-based size criteria.

42970161.label: Materials and methods
42970161.text: This retrospective study enrolled patients who underwent radical resection for colon cancer at Shantou Central Hospital between January 2015 and January 2019. All patients received radical resection followed by histopathological evaluation of regional lymph nodes. Preoperative computed tomography (CT) images were independently reviewed by two experienced radiologists using the Node-RADS scoring system. Inter-observer agreement was assessed, and diagnostic performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis.

42970161.label: Results
42970161.text: A total of 360 patients were included. Lymph node positivity was associated with several CT features, including nodal size, internal heterogeneity, necrosis, margin characteristics, fatty hilum status, and the Node-RADS score (all p < 0.05). The Node-RADS score demonstrated the highest diagnostic performance (area under the curve (AUC) = 0.835, 95% CI: 0.792-0.871) with an optimal cutoff of ≥3, good inter-observer reliability (intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) = 0.962), and higher discriminative ability than the conventional 10-mm size criterion (AUC 0.546; p < 0.05).

42970161.label: Conclusion
42970161.text: In this large retrospective cohort, contrast-enhanced CT-based Node-RADS demonstrated reliable diagnostic performance for preoperative assessment of LNM in colon cancer and outperformed the conventional size-based criterion. The good inter-observer agreement further supports the reproducibility and clinical feasibility of Node-RADS in routine clinical practice.

42970161.label: Key points
42970161.text: Question Can CT-based Node-RADS overcome the low sensitivity and underestimation of nodal metastasis associated with the conventional 10-mm short-axis criterion in preoperative colon cancer staging? Findings In 360 patients, Node-RADS at ≥3 achieved an AUC of 0.835, 96.6% sensitivity, and good interobserver agreement, outperforming the 10-mm criterion with fewer missed metastases. Critical relevance statement In 360 patients, Node-RADS at ≥3 achieved an AUC of 0.835, 96.6% sensitivity, and good interobserver agreement, outperforming the 10-mm criterion with fewer missed metastases.

42998161.label: Objectives
42998161.text: To evaluate technical and clinical success rates and complications of stent-grafting for hepatic artery bleeding or pseudoaneurysms.

42998161.label: Materials and methods
42998161.text: This single-centre retrospective study consecutively included 58 patients who underwent attempted stent-grafting for hepatic artery bleeding (n = 40) or pseudoaneurysm (n = 18) between January 2010 and June 2021.

42998161.label: Results
42998161.text: Technical success was achieved in 97% (56/58) of cases. Insufficient haemostasis after technical success was present in five cases (88% primary clinical success), decreasing to three cases after reintervention. In 3/5 cases, it was due to undersizing of the stent-graft, which occurred frequently, especially in vessel sizes ≥ 6 mm (n = 19, compared to the non-acute vessel diameter; n = 11, compared to the acute one). Median occlusion-free survival was 763 days. Patency rates were 81 ± 6% at 30 days and 56 ± 10% at two years. Early occlusion (≤ 30 days) was associated with significantly smaller stent-graft diameters (4.7 ± 0.7 mm vs 5.4 ± 0.7 mm; p = 0.014). In multivariate Cox regression analysis, a small diameter (4 mm) was confirmed as a risk factor for stent-graft occlusion (HR = 8.59, p = 0.006). Liver necrosis or liver failure due to insufficient collateralization occurred only in early occlusions. Median overall survival was 714 days. In 6/29 documented deaths, mortality was procedure-related (four because of insufficient haemostasis, with two after technical failure and two after technical success, and two because of fatal liver failure after stent-graft occlusion).

42998161.label: Conclusion
42998161.text: Stent-grafting is effective for managing hepatic artery bleeding, but precise sizing is crucial, as undersizing and small diameters increase the risk of inadequate haemostasis and occlusion.

42998161.label: Key points
42998161.text: Question What are the technical and clinical outcomes of stent-graft treatment for hepatic artery bleeding or pseudoaneurysm, and which factors influence these outcomes? Findings Stent-graft treatment achieved high technical and clinical success rates. Stent-graft undersizing and smaller stent-graft diameters were associated with inadequate haemostasis and occlusion. Clinical relevance Stent-graft treatment is an effective option for managing hepatic artery bleeding or pseudoaneurysm in critically ill patients. Accurate stent-graft sizing is a key determinant of clinical success.

43020361.label: Purpose
43020361.text: To determine if the proportion of patients receiving thoracic imaging, invasive diagnostic, or surgical procedures following community lung cancer screening (LCS) differed from that in the National Lung Screening Trial (NLST).

43020361.label: Methods
43020361.text: We compared the proportion of NLST participants and 2018 Medicare beneficiaries receiving imaging, invasive, or surgical procedures in the six months and one year following LCS, as well as lung cancer incidence and all-cause mortality. To create comparable cohorts, we used NLST chart abstraction data to impute information on procedures for participants with no abstraction.

43020361.label: Results
43020361.text: Within six months and one-year of LCS, NLST participants were significantly more likely to have at least one imaging test than Medicare beneficiaries (21.4 versus 16.5%); (difference=4.97%; 95% confidence limits (CL) 1.85%, 8.09) and 26.6% versus 22.3% (difference=4.28; 95% CL: 0.55, 8.02) respectively. NLST participants were significantly less likely to have an invasive or surgical procedure within six months of LCS (0.60 versus 4.64%; difference: -4.04% ; 95% CL: -5.23%, -2.84%) and (0.28 versus 1.51%; difference: -1.22% ; 95% CL: -1.80%, -0.65%) respectively, but neither differed significantly at one year. NLST had more cases of lung cancer diagnosed (3.83% [95% CL: 3.33,4.33] versus Medicare 2.26% [95%CL:1.51,3.01]). Mortality was not significantly different.

43020361.label: Conclusions
43020361.text: Medicare beneficiaries were less likely to have follow-up imaging within six months and one year of LCS, and they were more likely to undergo invasive diagnostic or surgical procedures at six months, but were not statistically significant at one year following LCS.

43020611.text: Head and neck cancer surgery requires autologous tissue transplants to reconstruct resection defects. The outcome of reconstructive surgery is often limited by perfusion-associated complications. To improve patient outcome, innovative approaches to detect perfusion deficits are essential for selecting the optimal free flap transplant donor site. Methods: A clinical pilot study was conducted that included 16 patients with head and neck cancer who were undergoing surgery and 10 healthy controls. Multispectral optoacoustic tomography (MSOT) was performed before surgery at the most common donor sites (radial forearm, latissimus dorsi, anterolateral thigh, and distal fibula). The biomarker of oxygen saturation in muscle and in the dermal layer was compared between healthy controls and patients and was correlated with clinical postsurgical outcomes. Results: MSOT examinations caused no adverse reactions and integrated smoothly into the clinical workflow. MSOT-derived muscle oxygen saturation showed significant differences between patients and healthy controls at all donor sites. These disparities became more pronounced under muscle provocation, revealing perfusion deficits that were previously not detected. Furthermore, exercise revealed side-to-side differences in hemoglobin saturation that exceeded 20%. Patients experiencing postoperative complications exhibited substantially reduced preoperative perfusion levels. Conclusion: In this clinical study, we demonstrated the feasibility of MSOT for donor site evaluation in autologous transplant surgery. Our findings highlight the potential of MSOT-derived hemoglobin metrics as functional imaging biomarkers for detection of perfusion deficits.
